turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Runners talk a lot about training and nutrition. You think sleep deserves more attention. Why?

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Because recovery happens mostly while we sleep. That's when the body repairs muscles and the brain processes what we've learned. If sleep is poor, training doesn't work as well.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Is there evidence that more sleep improves performance?

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Yes. One well-known study asked university basketball players to try to sleep about ten hours a night for several weeks. Their sprint times and shooting accuracy improved. Researchers call this approach sleep extension.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Ten hours sounds difficult for people with jobs.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Of course. But even adding thirty to sixty minutes can help. Many people are building up cumulative fatigue without noticing it. That's tiredness that adds up over many nights.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Does lack of sleep affect injuries?

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: It seems to. Several studies found that athletes who regularly sleep less than about eight hours have more injuries. Tired people have slower reactions and weaker concentration. That increases injury vulnerability.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Keep a regular bedtime, even on weekends. Avoid screens and caffeine late in the day. And during heavy training weeks, try to get to bed a bit earlier. Short naps of twenty minutes can also help. Think of sleep as part of your training plan, not something extra.
